title: Seventy-Nine Degrees | Silver
subtitle: Can a person fall in love with a piece of metal?
body:
**NOTE:** Some sensory-description writing exercises, inspired by teeth chilled by iced coffee in the morning.

================

## First Perspective: The Dental Filling

I am a silver filling embedded in the damaged part of the second-to-last tooth on the right side of her mouth.

I once thought I was an inanimate object, a substitute fitted into her mouth, a symbol of repair. But I understand ever more clearly that I am actually a secret door. She licks me, sucks me, rubs against me, not for cleanliness or comfort. Again and again, she confirms my existence, the existence of the only foreign object in her body.

After passing over me, the tip of her tongue always returns teasingly to lick my body again, once, twice. Trembling, I offer up a few silver ions in exchange for her satisfied, low sigh. Mixed with warm breath, that sound is like a rainstorm filled with fireworks bursting from her throat, sweeping through her whole mouth and covering all of me. Sometimes she suddenly coughs. She always thinks it is a mouth ulcer, but really I want so badly to be touched that I cannot help piercing a little of her mucous membrane. Unfortunately, the membrane does not always bleed, so I treasure every chance for blood to fall on my surface. It feels like an ocean current covering me after an undersea volcanic eruption—not foul, not scorching, only warm, continuously swallowing me. And saliva? Saliva is merely an indifferent lodger, pulling and stretching around me, preoccupied with its own shape. I hate its laziness, its rhythm, like a lover who only pretends. Excitedly, I dissolve more silver ions into her blood, slowly expanding within her.

Later, I began learning to seduce her tongue: while she spoke, while she swallowed, in the pauses of her breathing. I began to change shape. No longer a rounded filling, I grew gears, scales, and stitches. I was embedded between her teeth, but I could turn and pull. When she closed her mouth in silence, I slowly ground against the root of her tongue, waiting for her to bring me a suppressed yet pleasurable trailing sound.

“Are you sure you want this dental material removed?” I heard an unfamiliar voice.

“Mm.” The girl’s indistinct voice sounded. She had grown used to unclear articulation and breathing with a hint of sobbing.

Frantically I permeated every inch of her mouth with silver particles. She seemed to notice something amiss and straightened her throat, trying to prevent the endlessly surging saliva from invading deeper into her body. But she could not stop me. I passed through her soft palate, pierced the edge of her tonsil, and gripped the ends of her autonomic nerves. The old god fell; the new god took the throne.

A spinning sensation, and I saw the ceiling coming close to me, then receding.

I tilted my head slightly back, opened my mouth, and pointed out to the doctor the large wad of cotton filling it. Her faintly puzzled gaze crossed my face, but she still used forceps to remove the saliva-soaked cotton.

“I’ve changed my mind. Leave it in.” I spoke quickly, stood, and put on my coat. “Please still send me the bill. Sorry for the trouble.”

Without giving the doctor time to confirm again, I left the clinic. A faint sting came from the tip of my tongue. I pressed hard twice against the stinging place, then began gently licking it as though in consolation, obediently letting saliva pour forth, flow into my throat, and into the depths of my body.

A strange itch and contraction arose deep in my abdomen. Licking that newly born silver surface, I quietly listened to its first echo.

---

## Second Perspective
At first I did not feel anything wrong with the repaired tooth. Or perhaps I felt a little strangeness, but thought it normal after a filling. In any case, I did not take that faintly odd feeling to heart.

Until I realized that whenever I spoke, that tooth always touched my tongue before all the others—not a natural, occasional brush, but like a fingertip actively coming forward to meet it.

It took me a few days to admit that I liked it. I liked that little strangeness, that illogical existence, that foreign object that should not be in my body. It made me realize my body was not a closed system. It could be broken open, entered, tampered with.

I began touching it deliberately. Rubbing slowly with my tongue as I spoke; making my teeth avoid it while eating, just so it could float more distinctly in the saliva. Like a hook, it pulled me out of everyday numbness and hung me upon some deeper pleasure.

I brushed my teeth. Toothpaste foam collected along the silver’s edge. It did not retreat; instead, it seemed to enjoy it. Whenever the bristles brushed across it, it moved a little, as though asking for a kiss. I smiled, lowered my head to spit out the foam, rinsed, and turned off the light.

I began dreaming of it. In the dreams it was no longer embedded between my teeth, but slid slowly along the root of my tongue, like a warm beam of moonlight searching within me for a deeper exit. I told no one. I knew this was not “normal,” but its abnormality was precisely why I wanted to keep it.

I felt it moving—truly moving. Sometimes it swayed gently like a mass of mercury; sometimes it was like a swarm of tiny plankton building a nest deep in my mouth. I felt no fear, only an increasing desire for it to go further.

I began coughing; my speech slipped, even the word “I” began to falter. I knew it wanted my attention, and I was already waiting for it to take over more. But it was too restrained. It never grabbed or invaded, only waited for me to respond. Like a considerate but somewhat slow-witted lover, or a cautious choreographer who dared lean half a step forward only when I withdrew a little.

So I decided to go to the hospital. I did not truly want it removed; I only wanted to frighten it a little. I thought that if I pretended to end this relationship, it would become anxious, lose control, and begin to truly “possess” me.

I walked into the clinic, sat in the chair, and told the doctor in the indistinct manner of speech it liked that I wanted the silver removed.
The doctor asked, “Are you sure?”
I said, “Mm.”

I could feel its reaction. My throat contracted slightly, the root of my tongue grew hot, and saliva surged down like a tide. It was struggling, expanding, begging me to stay. Then it succeeded. It passed through my undefended soft palate and pierced the most sensitive point in my throat. My whole body jolted, as though split apart. A wave of dizziness.

When I opened my eyes again, I was no longer the same me.
“I’ve changed my mind. Leave it in.” In my mind I silently repeated the sentence it spoke, its tone light, as pleased as I felt at that moment. The doctor looked at us and asked no more, only nodded.

The air outside the clinic brought a restless heat. It reached out to stroke me: forceful at first, pain overpowering pleasure; then, as though changing its mind, slowly wandering through my whole body. Trembling, I gave up silver ions, faintly hearing its delighted laughter.

No, please do not think this is my defeat in a struggle for control of the body. It is the deepest kind of collaboration, one I have actively chosen. I am willing to be kept, controlled, caressed, filled.

I am willing to become the interface its tongue repeatedly strokes, the only response deep in its mouth, a secret desire impossible to speak of or relinquish.
